title: Same height, same volume.

beats.narration: Drill through a marble and through the Earth. Trim both leftover rings to the same height — they hold the same volume.
It's called the napkin-ring theorem. Punch a cylinder through any sphere and the leftover band's volume depends only on its height.

Slice the ring flat. Each slice is an annulus — sphere outer edge minus cylinder inner edge — and the R-squared cancels. What's left is pi times h-squared-over-four, minus z-squared. Add the slices, and the ring integrates to pi h cubed over six.
So a jeweller with a marble and a giant with a moon — same-height rings, same amount of stuff.

mechanism: Set the sphere at the origin and the cylinder on the z-axis. At height z the sphere's cross-section is a disk of area pi*(R^2 - z^2); the cylinder's cross-section is a disk of area pi*(R^2 - (h/2)^2), from Pythagoras applied to the cylinder radius. The napkin ring's slice at height z is the annulus between them, of area pi*((R^2 - z^2) - (R^2 - (h/2)^2)) = pi*((h/2)^2 - z^2). Every R has cancelled before integration. Integrating from z = -h/2 to z = h/2 gives V = pi*h^3/6, independent of the sphere's radius.

facts.claim: After a cylindrical hole is drilled through a sphere, the volume of the remaining band depends only on the band's height, not on the sphere's original radius.
facts.quote: It is a counterintuitive fact that this volume does not depend on the original sphere's radius but only on the resulting band's height.

facts.claim: The napkin-ring band's volume is a function of the band height h alone (not of the sphere radius R).
facts.quote: The volume of the band depends on h

facts.claim: The result is named the napkin-ring problem because the remaining band resembles a napkin ring.
facts.quote: The problem is so called because the part that remains resembles the shape of a napkin ring

facts.claim: An early study of this problem was written by the 17th-century Japanese mathematician Seki Kōwa.
facts.quote: An early study of this problem was written by 17th-century Japanese mathematician Seki Kōwa
